tEn: Designers Have a Superpower: Empathy in the AI Era
tZh: 设计师的超级力量：AI 时代中的同理心
sEn: A design leader shares how immersive field research and empathy can drive product innovation.
sZh: 一位设计领袖分享沉浸式实地研究与同理心如何驱动产品创新。

consensus.en: Empathy comes from experiencing your own product firsthand—even making deliveries—to truly understand user pain.
consensus.zh: 共情来自于亲身体验自己的产品——哪怕亲自去送货——从而真正理解用户的痛点。

consensus.en: Prototypes win arguments; they make ideas tangible and excite people far more than slide decks or PRDs.
consensus.zh: 原型能赢得争论；它让想法变得可感知，比幻灯片或 PRD 更能激发人们的热情。

consensus.en: AI tools give designers a superpower: building working prototypes quickly to explore and prove ideas.
consensus.zh: AI 工具赋予了设计师一种超能力：快速构建可运行的原型，去探索和验证想法。

consensus.en: Design leaders today must be player-coaches, staying hands-on while guiding smaller, flatter teams.
consensus.zh: 当今的设计领导者必须是球员兼教练：既保持亲自动手，又引导更小型、更扁平化的团队。

consensus.en: In 2026, designers need product thinking, scrappy research, and brand differentiation to remain valuable.
consensus.zh: 2026 年，设计师需要具备产品思维、务实研究和品牌差异化能力，才能持续创造价值。

consensus.en: Personal projects or 0-to-1 ventures demonstrate initiative, product thinking, and resilience that employers value.
consensus.zh: 个人项目或从 0 到 1 的创业经历，能展现主动性、产品思维和韧性，这正是雇主所看重的。

contrarian.en: When engineers or VPs say something can't be done, designers can now build it themselves with AI—so 'impossible' is less persuasive.
contrarian.zh: 当工程师或副总裁说某事做不到时，设计师现在可以借助 AI 自己把它做出来——所以『不可能』不再那么有说服力。

contrarian.en: Building software is no longer the bottleneck; growing an audience remains just as hard as ever.
contrarian.zh: 构建软件不再是瓶颈；增长受众仍然和以前一样困难。

contrarian.en: AI-generated designs tend to look alike; infusing brand soul early is essential to stand out.
contrarian.zh: AI 生成的设计往往千篇一律；尽早注入品牌灵魂是脱颖而出的关键。

contrarian.en: Even senior design leaders are expected to be hands-on, with interviews testing auto-layout and Figma skills.
contrarian.zh: 即使是资深设计领导者也被要求亲自动手，面试甚至可能考查 Auto Layout 和 Figma 技能。

contrarian.en: Relying solely on AI output is limiting; combining it with tools like Figma yields more distinctive results.
contrarian.zh: 单纯依赖 AI 输出会有局限；把它与 Figma 等工具结合，能产出更有差异化的结果。

contrarian.en: The cost of high-fidelity prototyping has dropped so much that leaders can prototype ideas between meetings in minutes.
contrarian.zh: 高保真原型制作成本已大幅下降，领导者甚至可以在会议间隙花几分钟把想法做出来。

turns.en: Like, that's such a fun and weird thing about this moment, is like you can't even claim to be an expert on any of this stuff, because literally like next month it's going to be totally different. 20% smarter. It's going to be able to do things you couldn't do today. So, there's a Cleo quote that I keep coming back to, where he talked about the aura of inevitability at early Facebook, and how when things are real and already kind of close to having the technology there, it's just so much harder to say no, we shouldn't do that. And all of a sudden, designers have the ability to bring the aura of ability to the table. And so, when you gave that, it's like, all right, shoot, we can't ignore this anymore. You know, it works. Like, he made this.
turns.zh: 这种事情的有趣和奇怪之处就在于，你甚至不能声称自己是这方面的专家，因为下个月情况就会完全不同，它会比现在聪明 20%，能做一些你今天做不到的事。所以，我总想起 Cleo 的一句引用，他说到早期 Facebook 有一种“不可避免的光环”，当事情是真实的，并且技术已经接近到位时，就很难再说“不，我们不应该这样做”。突然之间，设计师有能力把“能力的光环”带到桌面上。所以当你做出那个东西时，就像在说：好吧，糟糕，我们再也不能忽视它了。你知道，它是有效的。就像，他做出来了。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I'll add one thing to that. I'm remembering this part of my experience. At that time, I was one of the early and curious people in the AI space. Most of my design team that reported to me had not dabbled in vibe coding at all. We had one designer that was using Midjourney. That was the extent of AI practice on my team. I remember showing that example, that story to the designer that I was working with on online checkout with me, and she was just like, 'Holy expletive, I cannot believe that you, designer/manager, were able to make that, let alone in 15 minutes. And also, by the way, having the audacity to have a VP say no and then being like, actually yes, it's possible.' Right? So I think, again, maybe going back to the role of a manager thing, it's that courage of being able to sort of push on these tools, and dogfooding tools, instead of just sending them over to your team and hoping that they work.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。我想补充一点。我记得我经历中的这一段：当时我是 AI 领域里较早开始好奇的人之一。向我校报告的设计团队中，大多数人根本没碰过“氛围编程”。我们只有一个设计师在用 Midjourney。这就是我团队里 AI 实践的全部。我记得我把那个示例、那个故事给和我一起做在线结账的设计师看，她说：“我的天，我简直不敢相信，你，作为设计师/管理者，竟然能做出那个东西，更别说只花了 15 分钟。而且你还有胆量让副总裁说‘不’，然后你又说‘实际上，是的，这可行。’”对吧？所以我想，也许回到管理者的角色这个问题上，关键就是那种勇气：能够去推动这些工具，自己亲自试用，而不是直接把工具丢给团队，然后希望它们能行。

turns.en: I want to look at the state of the world today from a slightly different angle, because you recently navigated the job market as a leader, and I'm wondering if there was anything that felt clearly different this time around, or just other signals that you're seeing that kind of point to some of these ways that the landscape is shifting.
turns.zh: 我想从一个稍微不同的角度来看今天的世界状况，因为你最近以领导者的身份经历了求职市场。我很好奇，这次是否有任何让你感觉明显不同的地方，或者你还看到了哪些信号，能指向这些格局正在变化的方式。

turns.en: Totally. I mean, we talked a little bit about this sort of player-coach being maybe more in vogue right now. I can't think of a single leadership role that I've applied to — I've been a director for a number of roles, these are very senior positions — I can't think of a single one where they weren't expecting you to be hands-on. Period. Full stop. What that actually means is not clear in job descriptions. It sort of varies case by case. But I'll give you an example. When I was talking to an earlier stage startup, they literally put me on a call with an engineer in Eastern Europe and watched me use Figma to make sure that I knew how to use auto layout.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我们刚才聊到这种“player-coach”（既能带队伍又能亲自动手）的角色，也许现在更流行。我想不出我申请过的任何一个领导职位——我做过好几个总监职位，都是非常资深的职位——没有一个是不要你亲自动手的。就这么简单，句号。职位描述里其实没写清楚具体意味着什么，每个个案都不一样。但我举个例子：我和一家早期创业公司聊的时候，他们真的让我和东欧一位工程师通了电话，看我会不会用 Figma，以确保我懂怎么用自动布局。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Like literally, they gave me a design exercise — really literally was a test to see if I know how to use Figma, which by the way I did. Yay. I got, you know, I passed that. But yeah, that was a career first, you know. Likewise, I don't think the AI tools thing is necessarily something that people are putting on job descriptions, but people have definitely noticed my passion for building. They've noticed that between jobs, I was not only job searching, but also built an entire company from scratch called Matchmaker with my wife. I think seeing that somebody is not only kind of like a tinkerer of AI but literally can do end-to-end product development wearing the PM hat, the engineering hat, the design hat, and then also the entrepreneur hat — like, you know, all the other stuff, like incorporating the business in Delaware, paying the fees, figuring out your contract with your partners, all of that stuff. And I think that is something I've been saying for a minute, but some of the best design leaders are people that have spent some amount of time being entrepreneurs or working in early-stage companies, again because of that ownership thing. But I do think that I'm seeing more people that are finding what previously might have been called 'personal projects' as valuable, right? Like I call this a personal project because nobody hired me to build Matchmaker, but it was something that me and two co-founders created from scratch. It shows the kind of initiative and the resiliency of iterating through it. It shows product thinking, right? It shows technical savviness. It shows all of this stuff. And so I'm definitely seeing more companies that are looking at things that you built outside of work, not as extra credit, but as possible reasons to get jobs in addition to or even over traditional work experience.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。他们真的给了我一个设计练习——其实就是测试我会不会用 Figma，顺便说，我确实会。太好了，我通过了你懂吧。但那是职业生涯头一遭，你懂。同样，我觉得 AI 工具这类东西未必会写进职位描述，但人们肯定注意到了我对“做东西”的热情。他们注意到我在工作间隙不只是找工作，还和妻子一起从零创建了一家叫 Matchmaker 的完整公司。我觉得，看到一个人不只是 AI 的“玩票者”，而是真的能做端到端的产品开发，戴上产品经理帽子、工程师帽子、设计师帽子，然后还有创业者帽子——你知道，还要处理所有那些事情，比如在特拉华州注册公司、交费、确定与合伙人的合同，所有这些。这是我念叨过一阵子的观点，我认为一些最优秀的设计领导者，都是花过一些时间当创业者、或在早期公司工作过的人，还是因为那种主人翁意识。但我确实看到，越来越多的人把过去可能被称作“个人项目”的事情视为有价值的东西，对吧？我管这叫个人项目，因为没人雇我去做 Matchmaker，但它是我和两位联合创始人从零做出的。它展现了那种主动性和反复迭代的韧性。它展示了产品思维，对吧？展示了技术悟性，展示了所有这些。所以我确实看到越来越多的公司，把你工作之外做出的东西，不是当作加分项，而是当作获得工作的理由，甚至在传统工作经验之外或之上。

turns.en: You know, it's funny. I have a lot of design leaders in emails and Twitter DMs of people who are asking to come on the show. It's a different lens, but what I thought was so interesting about you was Matchmaker, too, for the exact same reason. It's like, oh man, not only do you have the pedigree, but talk about hands in the clay. There's no level of depth that you can get beyond building a totally new product and company going 0 to 1 on the whole thing, right? Like that says so much about who you are. So, I'm wondering if we can maybe even just get a little bit of behind the scenes. I'm curious what that process looked like. Maybe just were there specific lessons learned or hurdles that you had to overcome that you think people listening, who are inspired to do a similar journey or to just start building more, would benefit from seeing?
turns.zh: 你知道吗，这很有趣。我收到很多设计领导者的邮件和推特私信，他们想上节目。这虽然是另一个视角，但我觉得你身上特别有意思的也是 Matchmaker，原因一模一样。就像，天哪，你不仅有资历，而且简直是把手插在泥土里。没有什么比从 0 到 1 打造一个全新产品和公司更深的深度了，对吧？这非常说明你是谁。所以，我想我们能不能稍微看一看幕后。我很好奇这个过程是什么样子的。也许有没有一些具体的经验教训，或者你不得不克服的障碍？你觉得听众里那些受启发想要走类似旅程、或者想开始更多动手做东西的人，会从中受益？

turns.en: I think many of us probably have a lot of personal project ideas in our head — like problems that we have in our own lives that we want to solve. This was different. This was my wife Melanie. She's in marketing. She's been marketing for her whole career. And then she got the entrepreneurship bug and started an agency specifically on what's called brand partnerships. You know, 'I am an outdoor goods brand. I'm a luxury brand, right? I want to get more people to notice me and to build up a certain brand equity and to get people to buy my products, right?' Partnerships is like, okay, well, let's find other like-minded organizations or brands or creators, right? And find ways to work together so that we can have a win-win situation, leverage each other's audiences, so on and so forth. And so what Melanie and her partner noticed was that they were in all these Slack communities throughout the world, you know, that are all about marketing. And people were like, 'Hey, we're doing the Venice Biennale, you know, in a couple of months.'
turns.zh: 我想我们很多人脑子里都有很多个人项目的想法——比如我们生活中想解决的问题。但这次不一样。这次是我妻子 Melanie。她是做市场营销的，整个职业生涯都是做市场营销。然后她燃起了创业的热情，创办了一家专注于所谓“品牌合作”的机构。你想想，“我是一个户外用品品牌。我是一个奢侈品牌，对吧？我希望更多人注意到我，建立一定的品牌资产，让人们买我的产品，对吧？”品牌合作就是这样：好吧，让我们找其他志同道合的组织、品牌或创作者，对吧？然后找合作方式，实现双赢，互相借助对方的受众，等等等等。所以 Melanie 和她的合伙人注意到，他们身处世界各地所有这些关于营销的 Slack 社区里，你懂的。人们会说：“嘿，我们几个月后要做威尼斯双年展，你知道的。”
